54203-the-prisoners-of-mainz:
Alec Waugh's The Prisoners of Mainz was published by Chapman and Hall in London in 1919, with drawings by Captain Roussel, himself a prisoner at Mainz. Waugh had written The Loom of Youth before it. A ballade of dedication to his fellow-prisoner Chandler, dated at Boulogne on December 4, 1918, fronts the book, remembering eight months locked in the citadel, sipping the vintage of the Rhine.

Fourteen chapters tell the captivity in order: the great offensive, the way to the Rhine, Karlsruhe, the hungry days, parcels, the daily round, how we did not escape, armistice days, and freedom. The frontispiece is called The Doom of Youth. The dedication's verses recall the Ausgabe queues, and the barges bearing wine casks seawards past the alcove. Barbed wire tearing at loose breeches stands for hours less foul than fair in an unreal world behind the wire.
britannica-1911-abt-franz:
Franz Abt (1819-1885) was a German composer born at Eilenburg in Saxony, and his short Britannica biography traces a career built on song. He worked as kapellmeister, a director of music, at Bernburg and at Zurich, then held the same post at Brunswick for thirty years. He retired to Wiesbaden, where he died.

Songs brought Abt his fame. His solos and part-songs, written for several voices, sold and were sung all over Europe in the middle of the nineteenth century. The best of them entered Germany's recognized art-folk-music. The entry is candid about their limits, calling them easy and tuneful but short on lasting beauty.
britannica-1911-albert-i-elector-of-main:
Albert, elector and archbishop of Mainz, who lived from 1490 to 1545, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Younger son of John Cicero, elector of Brandenburg, he was born in June 1490 and studied at Frankfort-on-the-Oder. He entered the church and rose fast. In 1513 he became archbishop of Magdeburg, in 1514 elector of Mainz, and in 1518 a cardinal.

Buying those honours left Albert deep in debt to the Fuggers, the great banking house. Pope Leo X let him sell indulgences in his diocese to repay the loan, and Albert hired John Tetzel for the work. That sale helped spark the Reformation, giving Albert an indirect but potent influence on its course. His vote was courted by both Charles and Francis I at the imperial election of 1519. Later he defended Catholicism at Dessau, yet worked for peace more moderately than his brother Joachim.
britannica-1911-bregenz:
Bregenz, the Roman Brigantium, is the capital of the Austrian province of Vorarlberg, set at the south-east corner of the Lake of Constance. In 1900 it held 7595 people, German-speaking and Roman Catholic. The old town climbs a small hill topped by an old castle, while the newer town spreads on flat ground below it.

Trade on the lake made the place a port of weight, with grain as the chief good, plus cattle dealing and cloth from the cotton mills of Vorarlberg. The parish church of St Gall, a town museum rich in Roman finds, and rail links to Feldkirch and Munich all get note. Counts of Bregenz appear by the 10th century, and Habsburg buyers slowly took over their lands between 1375 and 1523.
britannica-1911-buddeus-johann-franz:
Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729) was a German Lutheran divine. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career and writings. He was born at Anklam, in Pomerania. His father was the town's pastor. He studied at Greifswald and at Wittenberg with distinction. He made a special study of languages, theology and history. In 1692 he became professor of Greek and Latin at Coburg.

In 1693 Buddeus moved to the university of Halle. There he held the chair of moral philosophy. In 1705 he became professor of theology at Jena. Jena held him in high esteem. In 1715 he became head of his faculty there. He also joined the Consistory, the church council. The entry lists his principal works at the close. They include a general historical lexicon, printed at Leipzig. They include a church history of the Old Testament. His writings on practical philosophy fill three volumes. His sacred miscellanies also fill three volumes.
britannica-1911-castelli-ignaz-franz:
Ignaz Franz Castelli (1781-1862) was an Austrian dramatist born in Vienna. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes he read law, then worked in state service. French invasions stirred him to write war songs for the army. One song was spread far by order of Archduke Charles.

Napoleon named him for ban, and he fled to Hungary for safety. Later trips to France and a Lower Austria post filled his middle years. He retired in 1842 to Lilienfeld, near his art collections in full. Plays that mocked Viennese folly made his name at home for years. Poems in the local dialect are held his most lasting work.
britannica-1911-coblenz:
Coblenz, or Koblenz, is a city and fortress of Germany, capital of the Prussian Rhine Province, 57 miles south-east from Cologne by rail. It stands pleasantly on the left bank of the Rhine at its confluence with the Mosel, from which circumstance it derived its ancient name Confluentes. Coblenz is a corruption of that Latin name, the entry explains. Its people numbered 31,669 in 1885 and 53,902 in 1905, a fast growth for a fortress town.

Strong modern forts crown the hills encircling the town on the west, and the citadel of Ehrenbreitstein stands on the opposite Rhine bank. The old city was triangular, bounded by the two rivers and a line of fortifications razed in 1890, letting the town expand. A bridge of boats 485 yards long and two railway bridges cross the Rhine. A Gothic freestone bridge of fourteen arches, built in 1344, spans the Mosel.
britannica-1911-delitzsch-franz:
Franz Delitzsch (1813-1890), a German Lutheran church scholar and student of the East, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Leipzig, he studied church learning and the tongues of the East at the university of his home town. In 1850 he became a full professor at Erlangen, where his school of scholars won wide fame. In 1867 he took a call to Leipzig, where he died.

The article stresses his deep care for the Jews and his hope for their turn to the Christian faith. He edited a journal for that cause, brought back an institute for Jewish studies, and founded a school to train men for the work. He also turned the New Testament into Hebrew. His grasp of rabbinic and talmudic books was so strong that men called him the Christian Talmudist.
britannica-1911-linz:
Linz, capital of Upper Austria and the seat of a bishop, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on the right bank of the Danube, west of Vienna by rail, with 58,000 people in 1900. An iron bridge joins it to the market town of Urfahr on the far bank, and Linz holds two cathedrals.

One cathedral was built in the late sixteen hundreds in rococo style, and the other, in early Gothic style, was begun in 1862. In the Capuchin church lies the tomb of Count Raimondo Montecucculi, who died at Linz in 1680. The town museum holds collections on the history of Upper Austria. In a main square stands a marble Trinity Column, raised in 1723 to mark the town's triple deliverance from war, fire and pestilence. Its works make tobacco, boats, farm tools and cloth, and its rail and river trade is brisk.
britannica-1911-natanz:
Natanz is the subject of a province entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a minor province of Persia, set in a hilly district between Isfahan and Kashan. It was held in fief by one family named in the entry. The province held eighty two villages and hamlets in all.

Its revenue and its population of about twenty three thousand are both given. It was divided into four districts, which the entry names in full. Natanz pears were famous across the whole country. An old high road between Kashan and Isfahan crossed its western part. That road fell out of use when new routes opened.
britannica-1911-oken-lorenz:
Lorenz Oken, who lived from 1779 to 1851, was a German naturalist. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Bohlsbach in Swabia. His true name was Lorenz Ockenfuss, shortened to Oken as a young lecturer. He studied at Würzburg, then went on to Göttingen. In 1802 he published a small work on the philosophy of nature. That book set him at the head of a German school.

The school is called natur-philosophie, or physio-philosophy. It carried Kant's principles from mind and morals into physical science. Fichte had pointed the path; Schelling entered on it. Oken went furthest, building a system of all nature from first principles. In his 1802 sketch he held that the animal classes picture the sense organs. Animals, he said, must be classed by that scheme. He kept to that claim all his life, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-sigel-franz:
Franz Sigel, a German born soldier who fought for the Union, fills a war life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Sinsheim in Baden in eighteen twenty four, he trained at a war school. He quit his post in eighteen forty seven after a duel death. When revolt broke out in Baden he led men on the rebel side. Flight to Switzerland and England came next in his path.

He sailed to America in eighteen fifty two and worked as a writer and teacher. At the start of the Civil War he raised German corps for the North. Wins at Pea Ridge made Missouri safe for the Union, the text says. He fought at Second Bull Run with high praise for his corps. A loss at New Market cost him his field post in eighteen sixty four.
britannica-1911-stuck-franz:
Franz Stuck (1863-), a German painter, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Tettenweis in Bavaria, he trained at the Munich Academy. He first made his name with drawings for a comic paper and with small designs for programmes and book ornament. He did not turn to painting in earnest until after 1889.

The article says his first picture that year, The Warder of Paradise, was a marked success. His style rests on a full mastery of design and is more like sculpture than painting. His dearest subjects come from myth and allegory, but he treats old themes in a way all his own. A bronze athlete by him stands in the state galleries of Berlin and Budapest. The entry lists his best known paintings and notes that he led the Munich breakaway group while holding a chair at the academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-heinz:
Joseph Heinz was a Swiss court painter to Emperor Rudolf II. Born at Basle in 1564, he likely trained under Hans Bock and taught himself by copying Hans Holbein the younger. He lived in Rome from 1585 to 1587 and settled in Bohemia in 1591. At once he became court painter at Prague, though he soon returned to Rome to copy antiques for the emperor.

His portraits and landscapes were his best work, including the family portrait at Berne and Rudolf II at Vienna. His landscapes, often too green, were simple in design and showed his deep study of light. The Dresden Gallery holds his Rape of Proserpine, Lot and His Daughters, and Ecce Homo. He died near Prague in 1609.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-linz:
Linz is the Catholic diocese covering Upper Austria, with its seat in the city of Linz. Emperor Joseph II carved it out of the huge Diocese of Passau in the 1780s. He hoped to curb Passau's power inside his lands, and Pope Pius VI gave the plan his reluctant backing in 1784.

Count von Herberstein, once Passau's deputy in Vienna, became the first bishop, and the bull of erection followed in January 1785. At its start the diocese held 26 deaneries and 404 parishes. Its church life soon felt Joseph's sweeping reforms: old devotions were cut back, churches were closed, and monasteries were shut. Later bishops, schools, and church building fill out a long record of a young see finding its feet under a meddling state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mainz:
Mainz was a German town and bishopric in Hesse. It once held an archbishop who was also an elector of the empire. A Celtic settlement stood near the site centuries before Christ. Its church and secular weight grew with its early archbishops. They built monasteries and ranked high among spiritual princes.

In the investiture struggle its archbishops could not stay neutral. As a free imperial town, Mainz thrived on linen and wool along the Rhine. Rival claimants tore it in the Stiftsfehde of 1461 to 1463. The Thirty Years' War then hit it hard. A modern diocese later gathered pieces of Mainz, Worms, Speyer, and Metz. Rome once refused a bishop chosen by the chapter. The present diocese matches the Grand Duchy of Hesse, save three places under Limburg, and its Romanesque cathedral leads its churches.
